{"id": "78:14/q02", "question": "What are the muʿṣirāt?", "turns_on": "The immediate source of rain ('from' clouds or sky) versus winds as the means of drawing it out; some explanations turn on whether the name describes imminent rainfall, squeezing, relief, or whirlwinds.", "positions": [{"id": "78:14/q02/p1", "position": "Rain-bearing clouds, heavy with water and ready to release it.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Nahhas, al-Qurtubi, and Ibn Kathir favor clouds because rain comes from them and the verse says 'from'; Ibn Kathir cites 30:48. Al-Farra, Ibn Qutayba, al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and others liken impending rain to a girl approaching menstruation; Abu al-Najm's verse is cited by al-Tha'labi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi. Al-Azhari disputes al-Farra's precise definition: Abu Ubayd's informants say a girl has reached maturity, al-Kisa'i says approaching twenty, and Ibn al-A'rabi says the moment of menstruation, relating it to seclusion/refuge. Al-Wahidi and Bursevi compare ready grain; al-Samin notes the active form suits imminence, since otherwise a passive participle would be expected for clouds pressed by winds, and reports al-Zamakhshari's entry-into-a-state explanation. Abu Ishaq derives the name from clouds squeezing out water; al-Mubarrad says they retain and release water gradually, with 'asr also meaning refuge. Ibn Kaysan links the term to relief and 12:49; al-Samin questions the form-IV derivation. Al-Azhari prefers rain clouds over whirlwinds, which do not bring rain. Al-Biqai adds that these clouds cool the sun and enable food and drink. Ibn Kathir reports al-Tabari's preference; Islahi says water-laden and rain-producing clouds do not differ essentially. Sibawayh cites a verse about Mayya's dwellings and rain clouds, and al-Jurjānī cites a poetic line in which al-muʿṣirāt disperse rain upon a deserted site. Al-Itqān explicitly identifies the muʿṣirāt as clouds. Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by Bint al-Shāṭiʾ, says clouds press one another so water emerges and cites al-Nābigha's poetry. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says that two clouds are not required by this gloss; rain-heavy clouds suffice. She cites al-Rāghib's definition as rain-saturated clouds, favors it from context and Quranic usage, and traces the root to pressure that extracts liquid, comparing 12:36, 12:49, and 2:266. Sibawayh cites a poem about a barren quarter in which al-muʿṣirāt are rain-bearing clouds that leave a wet stream."}, {"id": "78:14/q02/p2", "position": "Winds that squeeze, form, drive, or draw rain from clouds.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd cites 30:48 for winds raising clouds; al-Wahidi reports a rain-bringing wind, while al-Baghawi describes winds compressing clouds. Mujahid and others also describe whirlwinds or cyclonic winds. Al-Azhari, al-Tabrisi and Ibn al-Jawzi take min instrumentally as bi; al-Tabari objects that winds do not contain water, and al-Qurtubi prefers clouds as rain's immediate source. Al-Zamakhshari says winds form clouds and release moisture and cautiously reports that winds carry water from heaven. Al-Alusi says they compress clouds until rain falls. Bursevi rejects a causative derivation because winds themselves do the squeezing. Ibn Kathir cites reports from Ibn Abbas through al-Awfi and Ibn Abi Hatim. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ relates iʿṣār to the same root sense of pressure and describes it as a strong wind driving clouds, comparing 2:266."}, {"id": "78:14/q02/p3", "position": "The heavens or sky from which water descends.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan, Qatada and other named authorities identify the heavens. Al-Samin explains that water passes from heaven to clouds, as if the heavens enabled their pressing. Al-Nahhas, as quoted by al-Qurtubi, says sky, wind, and cloud explanations may converge because winds pollinate clouds; Ibn Kathir calls the heaven view unusual, while al-Alusi objects that the heavens are not squeezed and rejects the proposed reconciliation as strained."}, {"id": "78:14/q02/p4", "position": "Clouds specifically characterized by spiraling winds or whirlwinds.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba reports clouds possessing spiraling winds; al-Mu'arrikh and al-Mazini give the same description. Al-Wahidi's report from al-Mazini says a cloud has made an i'sar when a strong dust whirlwind rises; al-Alusi says such clouds necessarily bring rain. Al-Azhari counters that whirlwinds themselves are not rain-bearing. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports al-Rāghib's alternative that the clouds bring a whirlwind, but rejects it on the basis of the verse's context and Quranic usage, comparing 2:266 and 78:15–16."}, {"id": "78:14/q02/p5", "position": "Specifically the south wind.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi attributes this specification to Zayd ibn Aslam."}]}
{"id": "78:14/q03", "question": "How is “from” construed in the rain phrase?", "turns_on": "Whether min names the place water comes from or the winds that cause its release; the bi variant favors the latter.", "positions": [{"id": "78:14/q03/p1", "position": "It marks the source or starting point of the descending water.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Nahhas, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir use the ordinary 'from' sense to support clouds; al-Samin calls it the starting point. Al-Alusi reports an origin construal even when discussing the wind reading. Bursevi says descent from sky can pass through clouds."}, {"id": "78:14/q03/p2", "position": "It has an instrumental or causal force like bi, rain coming by means of winds.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi's al-Azhari, al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Tabatabai expressly explain min as bi for winds. Abu Hayyan calls it attributing rain to its cause; al-Samin distinguishes the causal bi reading from the starting-point min reading. Al-Alusi reports causal and origin construals."}, {"id": "78:14/q03/p3", "position": "Here min is adverbial (ẓarf), expressing the circumstance of descent from the clouds.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī calls min in the water-from-clouds phrase adverbial; he reports that some grammarians group this adverbial use among the meanings of bi."}]}
{"id": "78:14/q04", "question": "What preposition is read before al-muʿṣirāt?", "turns_on": "The codices' min is read as source; reported bi is generally taken as cause or instrument and often supports the wind interpretation.", "positions": [{"id": "78:14/q04/p1", "position": "The written codices read min al-muʿṣirāt.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi distinguishes the codices' min from reports of bi; al-Samin gives min a starting-point sense."}, {"id": "78:14/q04/p2", "position": "Some readers have bi-l-muʿṣirāt instead.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari reports this from Ikrima and Qatada; Ibn Atiyya names Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abbas, al-Fadl ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ikrima; Abu Hayyan adds Abd Allah ibn Yazid, and al-Samin names him. Al-Qurtubi names Ibn Abbas and Ikrima. Al-Jishumi compares 97:4. Durr reports Fadl ibn Abbas's codex, Ibn Abbas through Qatada, and Mujahid's bi reading. Al-Alusi calls bi causal or instrumental; Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say it supports winds, though al-Zamakhshari, reported by al-Samin, permits clouds too, like giving from or by one's hand."}]}
{"id": "78:14/q05", "question": "How is the rain brought down and sustained?", "turns_on": "Whether the notes describe wind transporting heavenly water, rain passing from heaven through clouds, or the sun raising terrestrial water into clouds.", "positions": [{"id": "78:14/q05/p1", "position": "Winds gather, carry, and drive water or water-filled clouds until rain falls.", "reasons": "Muqatil says winds draw water from the lowest heaven's sea of provisions (51:22), raise and join clouds, then release rain with wind. Ibn Masud says winds collect water and drive it into clouds until full like a milch camel; al-Tha'labi likens the falling scattered drops to water drawn from a pregnant she-camel. Durr gives Ibn Masud's full-udder image and heavy showers distributed by wind; Nasafi reports winds carrying sky water to clouds."}, {"id": "78:14/q05/p2", "position": "Rain descends from the heavens through clouds.", "reasons": "Qatada and al-Hasan report descent from the sky. Al-Samin explains the sky-to-cloud passage; Bursevi says this reconciles sky descent with cloud descent, and Nasafi relays a report of winds carrying sky water to clouds."}, {"id": "78:14/q05/p3", "position": "Celestial causes, including the sun lifting water from earth and sea, may produce rain clouds.", "reasons": "Bursevi offers this as another way to understand descent from the sky."}, {"id": "78:14/q05/p4", "position": "Rain-heavy clouds yield water under pressure; they may press one another, but two clouds are not required.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation that clouds press one another until water emerges, supported by a line of al-Nābigha. She treats this as a gloss rather than a necessary two-cloud restriction and says a rain-saturated cloud suffices."}]}

{"id": "78:14/q08", "question": "What variant form is reported for thajjāj?", "turns_on": "The reported final consonant or form varies, while the notes connect the forms with flowing water.", "positions": [{"id": "78:14/q08/p1", "position": "Al-Aʿraj reads thajjāḥan with ḥāʾ in place of jīm.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin report the reading; al-Alusi relates it to mathājiḥ, places where water gathers or runs together. {"id": "78:14/q09", "question": "What does this rain sign establish in the surah?", "turns_on": "The notes draw different lessons from rain: provision and resurrection, a reproductive image of creation, or a condition concerning the Hour.", "positions": [{"id": "78:14/q09/p1", "position": "Rain and its resulting growth show divine provision, power, and the certainty of resurrection and judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai says cooling rain yields food and drink; Islahi says sky-earth harmony displays monotheism, providence and accountability, while the signs of mercy, wisdom and power require a fixed reckoning. Ibn Ashur says the surah uses creation and humanity's first creation to prove resurrection, warn of punishment and contrast believers' reward; Muqatil says each sign is more astonishing than resurrection."}, {"id": "78:14/q09/p2", "position": "Sky, earth, water, and vegetation form a reproductive analogy.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai likens sky to male, earth to female, water to semen, and plants to offspring; he says springs and pools are implied."}, {"id": "78:14/q09/p3", "position": "The Hour cannot come while any water remains.", "reasons": "Muqatil adds this consequence while explaining the rain from the lowest heaven's sea of provisions and cites 51:22."}]}

{"id": "78:14/q14", "question": "What does māʾ mean here, and what is its lexical derivation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "78:14/q14/p1", "position": "It is rain in this verse; māʾ denotes life-sustaining flowing water and derives from m-w-h.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī defines water as a flowing substance sustaining animals and quenching thirst, and reports a definition calling it subtle, porous, and naturally seeking rest. {"id": "78:14/q15", "question": "How are ellipsis and case understood in poetic citations using al-muʿṣirāt?", "turns_on": "Whether the cited noun is accusative under an omitted verb or nominative in an identifying nominal clause.", "positions": [{"id": "78:14/q15/p1", "position": "An accusative noun may be governed by an omitted verb understood from context, such as 'I recall' before 'dwellings'.", "reasons": "Sibawayh supplies أذكر in Dhu al-Rumma's verse about Mayya's dwellings and rain clouds; he contrasts accusative الديار with the nominative and adduces omitted verbs in ولا زعماتك, familiar prohibitions, poetic accusatives, and formulas such as انتهوا خيرا لكم (4:171). He reports al-Khalīl's explanation of the latter as an understood second action, and notes that a parallel imperative can be explicit. Al-Jurjānī likewise supplies أذكر before accusative ديار and says omission can heighten eloquence. Sibawayh says familiar context and prior mention make omitted verbs recoverable: the accusative dates after كليهما can imply 'give me,' and a stated command can be less fixed than the customary ellipsis. Al-Khalīl, as reported by Sibawayh, explains that an imperative to stop implies a further action, 'enter what is better.' Sibawayh supplies omitted wishes after ألا رجل, an understood verb for the snake poem's accusatives, and implied remembering or finding in poems by Ibn Qumayʾa, al-Qaṭāmī, Ibn al-Ruqayyāt, and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Kilābī. He says nominative and accusative forms can reflect different understood thoughts, and restricts the خيرا ellipsis to a command rather than a statement or question."}, {"id": "78:14/q15/p2", "position": "A nominative noun may form an identifying nominal clause, with a demonstrative, subject, or predicate supplied from context.", "reasons": "Sibawayh reads nominative الديار as identification of Mayya's dwellings and reports Tamim speakers' supplied predicates in كلاهما وتمرا and كل شيء. Al-Jurjānī supplies ذاك or هو in ربع قواء أذاع المعصرات به and تلك before دار in another line; he notes the common omission of a subject at a fresh start. His teacher rejects taking الربع as a substitute for الطلل because a substitute must equal or exceed its antecedent, whereas a quarter is larger than a ruin trace. Sibawayh says some Arabs take كلاهما as 'both are mine,' followed by an implied request for dates; nominative الديار identifies the dwellings and nominative ربع can imply 'that is a quarter' or 'it is a quarter.' He says Ibn Abī Rabīʿa's parallel shows nominative and accusative reflect different unstated thoughts, and nominative زيد or عمرو can identify the man being wished for after ألا رجل."}, {"id": "78:14/q15/p3", "position": "A nominative noun can be the subject of an omitted verb supplied from preceding speech, rather than part of an identifying nominal clause.", "reasons": "Sibawayh reads nominative ضارع after لبيك يزيد with an understood 'let one weep for him.' He says a valley poem implies سقاها كل أجش from the preceding prayer. He also reports a nominative reading of شركاؤهم in 6:137 on the pattern of ضارع."}]}

{"id": "78:15/q04", "question": "What does ḥabb denote?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥabb is ordinary crop grain, defined by its use or cultivation, or pearls formed from rain at sea.", "positions": [{"id": "78:15/q04/p1", "position": "Edible grain or crop seeds, commonly harvested and chiefly human food.", "reasons": "Muqātil includes wheat, barley, and sesame. Naḥḥās and Ṭabrisī describe grain enclosed in husks; al-Ḍaḥḥāk, reported by Māwardī, calls it harvested seed in a husk; Ibn al-Jawzī reports al-Zajjāj's wider criterion of whatever is harvested. Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī's alternative, Ibn al-Jawzī's majority, Bayḍāwī, and Iṣlāḥī assign it to human food. Rāzī counts husked grain as one of three classes of terrestrial growth and says it is basic food. Qurṭubī, Nasafī, and Biqāʿī name wheat and barley; Biqāʿī calls it staple food. Abū Ḥayyān calls it staple food. Ālūsī says it is usually human food and more noble. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a collective for edible seeds, including wheat, barley, millet, corn, rice, and pulses. Ibn Kathīr says stored grain serves people and livestock; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the growth feeds people and other animals. The Study Quran names grain among the products God makes through rain."}, {"id": "78:15/q04/p2", "position": "Grain useful as food for animals.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya contrasts this grain with nabāt, grass used fresh by people or animals, and says both kinds of benefit are named."}, {"id": "78:15/q04/p3", "position": "What people sow.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports this as the counterpart to vegetation that people did not sow."}, {"id": "78:15/q04/p4", "position": "Pearls produced in the sea by rain.", "reasons": "Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī report ʿIkrima: each drop of heavenly rain produces a pearl in the sea or grass on land."}]}

{"id": "78:15/q06", "question": "What does nabāt denote?", "turns_on": "Whether nabāt is distinct grass or fodder, all vegetation including grain, or specifically unsown growth.", "positions": [{"id": "78:15/q06/p1", "position": "Vegetation such as grass, herbage, pasture, fodder, and other plants, especially growth eaten by animals.", "reasons": "Muqātil includes wild trees and grass of open country that renew yearly. Naḥḥās includes grass and fodder. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, reported by Māwardī, says pasture for grazing; ʿIkrima, reported by Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī, says each rain drop produces grass on land or a pearl at sea. Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī's alternative, Bayḍāwī, Biqāʿī, Ālūsī, and Iṣlāḥī assign vegetation to livestock, with Bayḍāwī specifying straw and grass. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the grass is eaten fresh by people or animals. Ṭabrisī includes herbage and other plants. Ibn al-Jawzī reports the majority's view that people and livestock eat it, and al-Zajjāj's description of pasture eaten by livestock. Rāzī says grasses lack husks or stems and cites 20:54 for grain and grass. Qurṭubī, Nasafī, and Ibn Kathīr describe fodder, pasture, or fresh edible plants; Ibn Kathīr adds varied fruit gardens. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it is useful vegetation whose seeds are not eaten, such as straw, clover, and grass. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the resulting food serves people and other animals. The Study Quran names plants among the products God makes through rain."}, {"id": "78:15/q06/p2", "position": "All growth, including grain itself.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says nabāt is broad enough to include every kind of growth, even the grain named before it."}, {"id": "78:15/q06/p3", "position": "Growth that people did not sow.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports this as the counterpart to grain that people sow."}]}
{"id": "78:15/q07", "question": "What is the grammatical origin of nabāt?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "78:15/q07/p1", "position": "It began as a verbal noun and became a conventional noun for useful vegetation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 71:17 in discussing its original verbal-noun use; in its conventional use he specifies vegetation whose seeds are not eaten, such as straw, clover, and grass."}]}
{"id": "78:15/q08", "question": "How do grain, vegetation, and gardens classify the earth's produce?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "78:15/q08/p1", "position": "Together they cover the kinds of growth brought out by rain.", "reasons": "Rāzī names three exhaustive terrestrial classes: grain with husks, grasses without husks or stems, and trees that form the gardens of the next verse; he says 20:54 names the first two. {"id": "78:16/q05", "question": "What does ‘alfāf’ describe about the gardens?", "turns_on": "Whether the description points chiefly to interwoven trees or crops, a combination of ground crops and upper trees, or the gardens' many colors.", "positions": [{"id": "78:16/q05/p1", "position": "Their trees, branches, or plants grow densely together and intertwine.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Zayd and the exegetes describe clustering, adjacent growth, or parts interwoven above one another; al-Ṭabarī says early interpreters agree on this sense. Abū ʿUbayda specifies no open space between trees; al-Qurṭubī mentions strong close branches, Ibn ʿAṭiyya fresh well-watered leaves and branches, and al-Biqāʿī abundant water. A poetic line cited by Ibn ʿAṭiyya uses alfāf for mingled groups and origins; al-Bayḍāwī also cites poetry. Ibn Kathīr compares diverse gardens sharing water with 13:4. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds that the density creates beauty even if farmers sometimes prefer spacing for yield. Sources vary between ‘intertwined,’ ‘clustered,’ and ‘wrapped’ in wording. {"id": "78:16/q06", "question": "What singular or formation is proposed for ‘alfāf’?", "turns_on": "Which singular is attested and which plural pattern can yield alfāf; authorities dispute the vowel, an intermediate plural, and whether deletion or a singularless plural is acceptable.", "positions": [{"id": "78:16/q06/p1", "position": "It is a plural of liff or laf, a word for a wrapped or dense garden.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, Abū ʿUbayda, al-Kisāʾī and most lexicographers are reported with this singular, usually with kasra; al-Ṭabarī prefers liff or lafīf since agreement on intertwining favors it over lafāʾ, which directly means thick. Al-Naḥḥās favors liff for the interpreters' gathered-garden sense. Abū Ḥayyān says the form is recorded by most lexicographers. Al-Samīn cites Abū ʿAlī al-Ṭūsī's ‘jannat liff’ line; al-Ālūsī cites al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī al-Ṭūsī's line with the same expression. Al-Ālūsī calls it the regular plural of a descriptive ‘wrapped’ word; Elmalılı calls it leff. Some sources leave the vowel unmarked. Itqān specifies that the singular liff has kasra on its first consonant."}, {"id": "78:16/q06/p2", "position": "It is a second plural: lafāʾ or a collective alf yields lif or laf, then alfāf.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba gives collective alf or lifāʾ as starting points; Abū al-ʿAbbās and al-Mubarrad give lifāʾ or lifa as the singular, then lif and alfāf. Al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Naḥḥās, al-Qurṭubī and al-Biqāʿī report versions of the two plural steps. Abū Ḥayyān describes liff as itself a plural of liff. Al-Zamakhsharī doubts the pattern because he knows no khudr/akhḍar or ḥumr/aḥmar parallel; al-Samīn replies that liff can behave like qufl and plural-of-plurals need not be regular. Al-Ālūsī finds the plural-of-plurals account unlikely and non-productive."}, {"id": "78:16/q06/p3", "position": "Its singular is lafīf, on the pattern sharīf/ashrāf.", "reasons": "Al-Qaffāl and al-Kisāʾī give the sharīf/ashrāf analogy; al-Samīn adds shahīd/ashhad and a poetic use of alifāf for interwoven groups. Al-Akhfash and Abū ʿUbayda are also cited for lafīf. Al-Ālūsī calls it a wrapped form on the faʿīl/afʿāl pattern."}, {"id": "78:16/q06/p4", "position": "It has no singular of the same form.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī compares awzāʿ and akhyāf, words for scattered or varied groups. Abū Ḥayyān replies that liff is attested and accepted by most lexicographers."}, {"id": "78:16/q06/p5", "position": "It is derived from multaffah by dropping added letters.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī proposes the clipped formation; al-Samīn objects that such deletion is chiefly discussed in diminutives and verbal nouns. Al-Kashf finds no comparable clipped plural, and al-Ālūsī calls it strained. Al-Bayḍāwī includes it among possible derivations."}, {"id": "78:16/q06/p6", "position": "Its singular is luff, with ḍamma.", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī allows the ḍamma form alongside liff; al-Mubarrad rejects that form and instead derives the word through lifa and lif. The Kasra form is separately disputed by Abū al-ʿAbbās as unattested."}, {"id": "78:16/q06/p7", "position": "Its singular is liffa, a densely grown garden.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya proposes liffa and describes its branches and leaves as intertwining in fresh, well-watered growth."}]}
{"id": "78:16/q07", "question": "What kinds of growth does the rain produce in this sequence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "78:16/q07/p1", "position": "Grain for food, grazing plants, and fruit-bearing or luxuriant gardens.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī explains grain as harvested seed in husks, including barley and dates, and nabāt as grazing fodder such as grasses and crops. Al-Rāzī divides terrestrial growth exhaustively into husked grain, stemless or huskless grasses, and orchard trees, linking the first two to 20:54. Ibn Kathīr adds fresh edible plants and gardens with varied fruits, colors, flavors, and scents; Iṣlāḥī distinguishes food for people, grass for cattle, and orchards. {"id": "78:16/q08", "question": "Why are grain, plants, and orchards mentioned in this order?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "78:16/q08/p1", "position": "Their order runs from essential human food to animal fodder, then less essential fruit.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says grain comes first as basic food, plants next for animals, and orchards last because fruit is less necessary."}]}
{"id": "78:16/q09", "question": "How does the passage picture the production of vegetation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "78:16/q09/p1", "position": "The sky and earth resemble a reproductive pair that produces vegetation through water.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī likens sky to male, earth to female, water to semen and plants to offspring; springs and pools are implied in the scene."}]}
{"id": "78:16/q10", "question": "What do these created signs establish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "78:16/q10/p1", "position": "God's purposeful power to resurrect people and bring them to judgment.", "reasons": "Abū Isḥāq and Ibn al-Jawzī say created growth is evidence for resurrection. {"id": "79:42/q05", "question": "What does 'the Hour' denote here, and how is the term used?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:42/q05/p1", "position": "Here the definite Hour is the decisive event of resurrection and the Afterlife.", "reasons": "Tabari calls it the Resurrection, as do Wahidi, Ibn Ashur, Biqai and others. In ordinary Arabic the definite noun can mean the present moment, and later named a timekeeping instrument. {"id": "79:42/q07", "question": "What does 'ayyāna' ask?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:42/q07/p1", "position": "It asks when, seeking the time of a future occurrence.", "reasons": "Zajjaj says it asks the time of the Hour's occurrence and arising. {"id": "79:42/q09", "question": "What does 'mursāhā' mean in the question?", "turns_on": "Whether mursā is the act of establishing the Hour, its endpoint or resting place, or the time fixed for that establishment; Alusi raises the when-versus-place difficulty for the endpoint gloss.", "positions": [{"id": "79:42/q09/p1", "position": "The Hour's occurrence or establishment: its arrival becomes fixed and manifest, like a ship reaching its mooring.", "reasons": "Farra explains irsa' through a moving ship that stops, and compares the standing of justice or truth; Tabari repeats the ship, manifestation and fixedness comparison. {"id": "79:42/q10", "question": "How does this question connect with the surrounding passage and sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:42/q10/p1", "position": "After establishing resurrection and its consequences, the sūra turns to the deniers' demand for its date and the reply that God knows it.", "reasons": "Razi says the preceding argument established possibility and reality of resurrection and described its general and moral states.
